blocks.x: Hidden in the acknowledgements of the writer Lars Anderson's new book, Brady: An American Story and The Price of Greatness, is a grand romantic gesture: the first letter of each paragraph, Anderson revealed to me with a bashful smile just before the book's publication, spells out a marriage proposal to his girlfriend. (She said yes.)

On the surface, this has very little to do with Tom Brady, Anderson's outsized and polarizing subject, a man so genetically blessed and good at playing quarterback that he's despised by large swaths of the American public for the crime of chronic winning. But Brady, more so than any other biography of the seven-time Super Bowl champ, doubles as an audit of his marriage to supermodel Gisele Bündchen. Reading Anderson's account of their slow-burn separation, framed here as the result of Brady's maniacal devotion to sport, one sees why the author might have felt compelled to pop the question himself. What emerges in Brady is a portrait of a man too committed to football and the neurotic project of self-mastery to notice that his family needed him.

Make no mistake: Anderson's biography is more than a gossipy account of how the world's most photogenic union fell apart. The former Sports Illustrated writer has conducted over 350 interviews with individuals in Brady's orbit, a reportorial feat that yields a number of remarkable and illustrative anecdotes from former teammates and coaches. You may not know, for instance, that the man famous for pioneering pliability exercises and plant-based diets was once a prodigious chugger of beer. Or that he sometimes transforms into a character known as “Psycho Tom,” who Anderson describes as “mean, angry, demanding, blunt, a lover of the words fuck and shit.” Or that he and the famously savage New England Patriots safety Rodney Harrison once engaged in a weeklong turf war, each one arriving to the team facility a little earlier each morning to demonstrate their unsurpassable work ethic. Brady, with “the fire of an Irishman and the quiet composure of a Norwegian,” ultimately prevailed.

Ahead of the book's publication, Anderson joined GQ to talk about how Brady's example supercharged his own writing routine, taking on the mother of all sports biography subjects, and what might compel a man to choose football over the “most beautiful woman in the history of the world.”
Hey there, Lars. How’s it going?
I'm terrific. Terrific, terrific, terrific. Thank you so much for your interest in my book.
It’s out this week. It’s not your first rodeo, but I'm curious how you're feeling about it.

It's just completely out of my control and I'm not really paying too much attention. I know there's really high expectations for this particular book, and I certainly worked harder on it than any book I've ever worked on in my life.
Is that right?

Oh, easily. My literary agent framed it to me like, "You've written all these wonderful books, but this really is your shot." And very quickly, I tried to match the level of obsession that Tom has. I'm a morning writer, but I never had gotten up at four every morning, and that's what I did. I usually could only write with sustained concentration for 45 minutes and then I'd have to take a break. But I was going six hours at a time before I'd need a break. That's the level of care I put into it.

Well, I’m curious to know more about the inception of the project, because a lot of ink has been spilled about Tom Brady. When you set out to write this book, was there some particular part of his story or persona you felt had been insufficiently unpacked?

Several books ago, I wrote The Quarterback Whisperer with Bruce Arians, who was the head coach of the Arizona Cardinals at the time. And then Bruce becomes Tampa Bay’s head coach and they win the championship with Tom. Right after that, within days, Bruce and I essentially got a book deal and I had to write a quick book in 12 weeks. And in researching that and talking to so many people, I thought that there's more to Tom here than a lot of people understand.

Interestingly, my only interaction with Tom—Bruce basically ordered him to talk to me—was on my 50th birthday. I see a car pull in the driveway. My mom and my brother are walking towards the house to surprise me and, right at that moment, my phone lights up. It’s Tom Brady. I said, "Tom, I can't believe I'm going to say this, but I can't talk right now. My mom is here." And he was so gracious. He just very gently said, "Lars, go be with your family. We'll get it done." And of course, we never got it done, and that was literally the only time we ever talked. But through all of that, through knowing Bruce and getting a close look at Tom through Bruce's eyes, I thought there was something here. So when my agent and I were contemplating what to do, she just called me one day and said, "Brady." My initial response was, "Are you fucking kidding me? That is the tallest of mountains to climb." But she thought that I was in a unique position because of the relationships that I had formed.

After we got the deal, the first person I called was Armen Keteyian, who had co-written the Tiger Woods book with Jeff Benedict. I'm like, "How the fuck am I going to do this? What did you guys do right when you got the deal with Tiger?" And he said, "We spent a year making a detailed timeline of his life." So that's what I did—I went year by year, and I started to forge the narrative.

The question also becomes, “Where do you want to start the book?” And the only reason I started it with the blind date [with Bündchen, in 2006] was because I asked myself, “What was the point away from football where the stakes were the highest for Tom, where there was the most emotional tension?” Framing it that way seemed natural to me. Now, did I ever see myself as someone getting into the gossip game, the tabloid shit? Absolutely not. And I'm blindsided, to be honest. I didn't think that people would be so interested in the details of what went wrong there.
Yeah, the book was in TMZ the other day.

Hands on bible, man, I was not expecting this. But it distills it to this fundamental question of, this is the most beautiful woman by many metrics in the history of the world. She's been on more magazine covers, made more money, it goes on and on. And yet he chose a game over her. Why is that? Well, now you're getting into some deep psychological ground that is worthy of ginormous exploration.

That leads to my next question. Of course, it’s not incumbent on you to make a judgment call as to whether or not it was worth it for Brady. But he won seven rings, you know? By most accounts, he’s the greatest quarterback who’s ever played the game. So while I was reading, I imagined he'd say it was worth it.

I think if Tom could do it over again, he wouldn't have come back for that final season, but does that mean the marriage could have been saved? I have no idea. But there also was a real sense in the Buccaneers' locker room that they had a team that could win it all. Clyde Christensen, who was a quarterback coach in Tampa and a wonderful man said, "We were hoping that Tom would actually come out of retirement again, because we think we could have gotten number eight that year." But Tom told him, "Look, because of the divorce, it's changing so much and I don't know how I'm going to navigate this new portion of my life." So ultimately, he did walk away for his kids. But if they didn't have kids, I'm certain he would still be playing. There's no doubt in my mind.
One heartbreaking part of the book was when you suggest that was not the father to his kids that his dad was to him.

Oh, God. It's heartbreaking. You see early on in the book what a great dad Tom Sr. is. In my view, he's the third most important character in this entire book, and just a model of what a dedicated father is. And Tom knows that he didn't measure up to that. But it's a question that all of us can ask ourselves: What are we willing to sacrifice if we have the opportunity to be the very best at what we do?

On that note, and the pain that Tom was going through, I've been through two divorces, so I'm not exactly a go-to guy on how to make a successful marriage. But I think every author brings their own experience and perspective, even to narrative nonfiction. And I believe that the reason I was able to write that really descriptive scene of him in the locker room—they just lost a game, but clearly something else was going on—was because I tried just to imagine how I'd feel. He's in full uniform with his head down, just in a catatonic state. And the next morning, the divorce is finalized.

Right. To shift gears a bit, I want to ask you about Brady as a subject. There’s this idea, argued most famously in David Foster Wallace’s essay about reading Tracy Austin’s memoir, that athletes are really ill-equipped to speak to their own greatness. They have this tunnel vision that makes them remarkable at sports but prevents them from offering much insight about why they're so good. That doesn’t seem to be the case with Tom Brady.

I think one of the hallmarks of a good biographer or profile writer for magazines is to reveal truths about the subject that the subject themselves cannot see. Because how we see ourselves is not necessarily how others view us, right? And I found Tom to be just utterly fascinating, probably the most interesting person I've ever studied. And that made writing the book easier. I'm good friends with Jeff Pearlman, who’s written books about guys he ends up just despising, like Barry Bonds and Roger Clemens. And then it becomes a heavy lift: "God, I’ve got to go back into this guy's brain today." But with Tom, there's so much emotional, intellectual depth to him.

He was the youngest of four, with three older sisters, and his dad's a traveling salesman, so he’s gone a lot. So Tom was raised in a household of women, and his sisters would put a pop of red lipstick on him, do his toenails, all that. But how did that influence his future leadership? Well, I think you can draw a straight line. He is a relationship-driven leader, and he’s just so good at cultivating relationships. Out of all the people we interviewed—350-plus, or whatever it was—even those who had axes to grind did not say a negative word about Tom's character. Everybody said Bill Clinton had this ability to make whoever he was talking to feel like the most special person in the world. Well, Tom has that ability too. Plus, he's smart, he's shrewd, he's calculating, and he just knows how to win over people and win over players. Now post-career, which I really don't cover in the book, he's made some curious decisions, that's for sure.

The book is just jam-packed with some amazing anecdotes from his childhood, his high school years, his time at Michigan. When you reached out to folks who hadn’t seen Tom in decades, were they mostly willing to talk about him candidly?

I'll say this: as far as I know, nobody said, "We can't talk to you because Tom told us not to." I don't think he blocked anybody. Of course, some people that we reached out to simply didn't get back to us, but a lot of people did. We cast a very wide net going all the way back to his years at San Mateo [High School]. I'm always interested in childhoods and what is it that causes these things to happen in our own lives as we get older.
I loved learning about his intolerance for chewing tobacco, or how stung he was by the quarterback competition with Drew Henson in college.

I love the beer chugging stuff, man. I always just try to pick the most compelling scenes. I consider myself a scene writer, and I'm such a huge believer in the power of anecdotes to illustrate larger truths. I mean, I never set out to write about Tom Brady. I had no thoughts about him, positive or negative, other than that one silly interaction we had where he seemed perfectly polite. I had been at a couple events with him. I'd been in the locker room several times for Sports Illustrated. But I had no preconceived notions. And maybe some reporters in Boston would disagree, but I think to give someone like Tom the fairest treatment, it almost takes somebody parachuting in from the outside to examine everything with fresh eyes.

You watched loads of tape to write this book, and you do a nice job of recreating particular games, even certain throws. Is there one that you think is most illustrative of Tom’s greatness—a game, a drive, even a pass?

It was the throw he missed to Randy Moss. The second-to-last play of the Super Bowl against the Giants. Corey Webster, who I knew at LSU, made a hell of a play and just barely got his fingertips on it. I mean, he threw that thing 78 yards. And I can almost guarantee you that that’s the one throw Brady remembers the most out of his NFL career. Not a completion, but that missed throw, because it could have been the greatest play in NFL history.
Last question, Lars. What do you think Brady would think about this portrait of him? Do you care?

I think the person's opinion I care about most is Tom Sr. I could just be the asshole journalist saying, "I don't give a fuck." But I feel like I spent three years with this family, and this is a good family. These are good people, and I hope that they think that I gave everyone a fair, balanced, accurate presentation. And of course, when I'm recreating scenes based on other people's recollections, there's no question that certain things will be a tick off here or there, right? Because I'm recreating stuff to the best of my ability using people's memories of events that took place a long time ago. But that being the case, I would be curious to hear what his dad had to say about it.
